questions_asked: When a Great Lakes lake's water level is getting dangerously low for big ships to pass through, which group suffers most: the shippers, the towns along the shore, or the power plants?
You said shippers lose most when water is low. Do ship operators get paid or penalized for running light at shallow levels, or do they simply carry less?
If a lake sits near the top of its usual annual range, what do the dam operators usually do to the outflow?
You said releases are capped by downstream limits. In practice, does the downstream flooding concern stop operators from releasing much, or is it a rare worry?
During a spring snowmelt surge, which matters more to operators that day: getting the lake level down fast, or not flooding the river below?
If a forecast badly overestimates a spring surge and operators hold back water, what typically happens to the lake and to downstream river towns?
When ice jams form on the St. Lawrence in winter, what do they usually do to the river's flow and to the upstream water level?
How often are water-level forecasts in this system off enough to matter, and which direction do they more often err, too wet or too dry?
When operators set the planned water level for a lake for the year ahead, how confident are they in sticking to that plan?
Among the five Great Lakes, which one do people most often blame on dam releases for problems that are really caused by weather?
expert_answers: The shippers suffer most. Low water directly cuts the controlling depth in connecting channels and locks, forcing cargo light-loading (reduced tonnage per trip) or halting transits — an immediate, unavoidable economic hit. Shore towns and property owners actually benefit from low water (less flooding, less shoreline erosion), and hydropower plants lose only some head/efficiency, a partial and gradual loss rather than a hard constraint. So the binding, first-order loser is commercial shipping.

They simply carry less — and that is the penalty. Shipping is priced largely per unit of cargo moved, so a light-loaded vessel spreads the same trip cost (fuel, crew, time, lockage) over fewer tonnes, raising cost per tonne. Under typical bulk freight contracts the carrier absorbs this: the operator is not separately compensated for running light, and if a charter guarantees a minimum tonnage the operator may owe the shortfall or deadfreight. So the loss shows up as reduced revenue per trip and higher unit cost, not as a direct fine for shallow draft.

They increase outflow — release more water downstream — to draw the level back down toward the target range. When a lake is near the top of its range, the standard operating policy is to pass more water through the control structure (open gates wider, run more through the hydropower/navigation works) so the level does not continue rising into flood-risk territory. The release is constrained by downstream conditions: operators will not push outflow so high that it floods the downstream lake or river reach, so the response is "release more, up to the downstream limit," not unlimited drawdown.

It is a real and frequently binding constraint, not a rare worry — but it usually caps releases rather than stopping them.

The two control structures sit in series: Compensating Works at Sault Ste. Marie releases into the St. Marys River and, ultimately, the lower lakes; Moses-Saunders at Cornwall releases into the St. Lawrence, whose downstream reach includes Montreal. Operators routinely hold releases below what the upstream lake's own level would call for, because pushing more water downstream would raise levels in the receiving lake or river reach. The classic case is Lake Ontario: outflow is limited by conditions at Montreal, so Ontario can be held above its desired level precisely because downstream flooding risk forbids a larger release.

So the practical pattern is "release more, but stop at the downstream limit" — the cap is active often enough that it is a standard part of operating decisions, especially in wet periods, rather than an exceptional event.

Not flooding the river below matters more that day.

During a spring snowmelt surge the downstream reach is already rising from the same runoff, so its margin to flood is at its smallest. Operators will hold or cut the release even when the upstream lake is climbing, because a flood in the downstream river reach (e.g., Montreal below Moses-Saunders) is an immediate, damaging, hard-to-reverse event, whereas the upstream lake level is a slower, partially self-correcting variable that can be drawn down later once the surge passes.

So the ordering is: downstream flood protection is the binding constraint; getting the lake down fast is the secondary objective, pursued only up to the downstream limit.

The lake ends up higher than intended — operators held back water that never arrived, so the upstream lake stays elevated (or rises) above its target, and the drawdown they planned is delayed until the surge is confirmed smaller and they can release more.

Downstream river towns get the opposite of what was feared: because the release was cut, they see lower-than-expected flows and levels, so the flood risk they were being protected against does not materialize. The cost of the error is therefore shifted upstream — shoreline flooding/erosion risk on the lake — rather than realized downstream.

The asymmetry matters: the mistake is usually recoverable, since the held-back water can be released later once the forecast is corrected, but the upstream lake may sit high for weeks and the missed drawdown can compound if wet conditions continue.

Ice jams raise the upstream water level and reduce the river's flow capacity.

A jam is a physical blockage: it constricts the channel cross-section, so the same discharge backs up behind it, raising water levels upstream (and often causing local flooding of low-lying areas). The effective conveyance drops, so for a given upstream level the river carries less water past the jam — flow through the constricted reach is throttled. Downstream of the jam, flow can drop sharply while the jam holds, then surge when it releases.

For the control system this means the St. Lawrence outflow at Cornwall can be impeded by ice, so Lake Ontario's level can rise even without extra release — the downstream "limit" becomes tighter and less predictable in winter.

Forecast errors large enough to change an operating decision are common — a routine occurrence in a system driven by precipitation, snowmelt, and ice, not a rare event. In any given season operators are frequently adjusting releases as forecasts are revised.

Direction: the errors are roughly symmetric over the long run, but the consequential ones are not evenly split. The errors that *matter* most are overestimates of incoming water (too wet) in spring, because they cause operators to hold back releases and leave the lake high — the asymmetry noted earlier. Underestimates (too dry) also occur and lead to over-release, but the resulting downstream flood risk is usually caught and corrected faster.

So: frequent enough to matter, with the damaging tail skewed toward "too wet" forecasts in the snowmelt season. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise frequency.

They are not confident in the sense of committing to a fixed number — the "plan" is a target range, not a set level, and it is routinely revised within the year.

Operators set a desired operating range (a band, typically on the order of tens of centimeters to a meter wide) and adjust releases continuously to keep the lake inside it. Deviations of two to three feet are explicitly noted in the problem as consequential, so the band is narrow relative to the variability they face.

Confidence in hitting the band is moderate at best. Precipitation, snowmelt, ice, and forecast error are outside their control, and the downstream flood constraint can force them to hold water against the upstream target. In practice they expect to miss the target in wet spring seasons and to be constrained by downstream limits in others. The plan is a guide for release decisions, not a commitment they expect to meet exactly.

Lake Ontario.

It is the lake whose outflow is directly controlled by Moses-Saunders Dam at Cornwall, so it is the one where dam releases are a visible, named lever — and it is the lake with the most active shoreline-stakeholder controversy (the IJC's Lake Ontario–St. Lawrence River Board exists largely for this). When Ontario sits high or low, property owners and municipalities attribute it to release decisions, even though the dominant drivers are precipitation, snowmelt, evaporation, and ice — and even though the downstream Montreal flood constraint often forces operators to hold water against Ontario's own target. The other four lakes have no comparable single control structure at their outlet, so there is no obvious dam to blame.
